entry.dc:title: Controlled blasting operations and high wall stability in surface mining in Australia
entry.dc:creator: Pilcher B.
entry.dc:description: This paper will present the controlled blasting methods used in surface operations in Australia and mentions some of the design guidelines used in maintaining pit wall stability. The methods will include cushion blasting, presplitting, postsplitting and the use of these methods with production blasts.

entry.dc:title: Advantageous use of long-distance exploration in surface mining as exemplified by the Lusatian brown coal mining industry
entry.dc:creator: Drebenstedt C.
entry.dc:description: Brown coal mining encroaches on the immediate environment like no other process of human activity. It is characteristic of the mining process in particular that it has an effect on nature over a large area and also over a long period of time. In order to lessen and compensate the effects of this encroachment by the mining industry, measures are adopted already during the mining process which aim, above all, to reduce the effects resulting from changed ground-water conditions and to ensure the creation of local abiotic features on the dumps and tips so that stable natural conditions can be established again after the cessation of mining operations. Long-distance exploration is a valuable aid for determining and recording the manifold and complicated relationships between mining and the environment. In this way the geometry and characteristic features of the objects in question can be determined. From sequential photographs showing changes in nature conclusions can be drawn, for instance, as to whether such changes have been caused by mining, as to the extent to which safety and preservation measures are effective, and whether recultivation can be carried out systematically. Together with other data on the area in question, long-distance exploration data can be stored in geo-information systems and can be evaluated and used very effectively for planning and monitoring purposes.

entry.dc:title: Developments in the analysis of footwall slopes in surface coal mining
entry.dc:creator: Stead D.
entry.dc:description: Surface mining of coal, particularly in areas of mountainous topography, often involves the formation of extensive footwall slopes parallel to the strata dip. Due to structural deformation steep dips on the limbs of folds may be encountered in association with thrust faults, jointing and residual shear strength conditions. Such an environment necessitates a rigorous assessment of footwall stability in order to ensure safe and economic exploitation of the coal. This paper provides a detailed review of the factors influencing footwall slope instability in surface coal mining and the major instability mechanisms which have been recognized within the published literature. The analysis of footwalls in the design stage and the back analysis of footwall slope failures has in general been undertaken using predominantly two-dimensional limit equilibrium techniques often incorporating a simplistic elastic column analysis. The application of numerical modelling techniques to surface coal mine footwalls has received little attention. In this paper the authors attempt to illustrate the potential for investigating footwall failure mechanisms and stability using principally the distinct element method. © 1997 Elsevier Science B.V.
entry.authkeywords: Analysis of footwall slopes | Mountainous topography | Surface coal mining | Two-dimensional limit equilibrium technique

entry.dc:title: Retreat of halophytes in the Czech Republic: Agricultural, mining, and urbanization effects: [The Case of Dentated Melilot - Melilotus dentata (Fabaceae)]
entry.dc:creator: Nováková J.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Agricultural and Environmental Ethics
entry.dc:description: As a result of expanding human pressures, the heterogeneity of a formerly diverse landscape has been reduced and the richness of animal and plant species has decreased. Some particular stand types and their species are especially connected with impoverishment caused by man's activities. Halophyte Dentated Melilot (Melilotus dentata, Fabaceae) is one of such species, which is vanishing apparently as a result of intensive agriculture, surface mining, and urbanization. The data on its distribution were compiled from herbarium specimens, literature, and the author's own field observations. The distribution was mapped separately for four periods: up to 1900, 1901-1945, 1946-1975, and after 1975. The trend in reduction of localities was documented. At the same time, their environmental quality was changing as well. Basically, the salt marshes in their original areal extent and their former species richness have disappeared. Current localities of M. dentata include poor fragments of the salt marshes mentioned above and secondary stands, e.g. ruderal places inside villages, strips along drainage ditches, paths, railway lines, fields, etc.
entry.authkeywords: Biodiversity | Halophytes | Land use | Melilotus dentata | Salt marshes

entry.dc:title: Getting maximum yield from surface mining land by reclaiming pits with municipal waste
entry.dc:creator: Lee Aston R.
entry.dc:description: Surface mines, particularly those of construction minerals, are prime sites for solid waste depositories. Annual surface mining amply creates sufficient void space to accommodate annual volumes of waste generated. Open pits should be used as landfills to accomplish complete reclamation of a majority of mined voids, restoring the land to beneficial surface re-use, thereby conserving land. Present day technology can make almost any pit safe from landfill leachate contaminating groundwaters. Successful examples are given in three Anglo nations. The combining of two earth-disturbing industries, surface mining and landfilling, is advocated. Landfilling problems and pit preparation are discussed. Voluntary reclamation by landfilling and regulatory dual purpose permitting for mining and landfilling is proposed. The public's urgent need for waste disposal space is simultaneously resolved. Fully restored mined lands create increased land values by highly profitable landfilling. Industry and environmentalists should rejoice.

entry.dc:title: Different types of belt conveyors and their applications in surface mines
entry.dc:creator: Kesimal A.
entry.dc:description: Due to its nature, open-cast mining requires a variety of conveying systems able to offer: high capacity to suit the mine's throughput, flexibility by means of extensible or shiftable machines, to accommodate a continuously moving quarry-face, uphill conveying at steep angles in order to adapt to the mine grades, downhill conveying, accommodation of a variety of material sizes, and suitability for long hauls over difficult terrain. Most of the transportation studies related to surface mining will evaluate the economics of the belt conveying technology versus truck hauling. Sometimes, depending on specific local conditions, railway based transport will be considered. As conveyor technology advances and the operators increasingly take a long-term approach, flexible and reliable belt conveying systems become the method of choice in such operations. In this paper, presently and commonly used belt conveyors in surface mining have been reviewed.

entry.dc:title: An overview of diesel particulate exposures and control technology in the u.S. mining industry
entry.dc:creator: Haney R.A.
entry.dc:description: Studies of diesel particulate exposures in the U.S. mining industry indicate that diesel particulate exposures in surface mining operations are generally less than 0.2 mg/m<sup>3</sup>. Average diesel particulate exposures in underground coal mines using diesel-powered equipment ranged from 0.1 to 2.1 mg/m3. Average diesel particulate exposures in underground metal and nonmetal mines ranged from 0.3 to 1.6 mg/m<sup>3</sup>. The purpose of this article is to provide an overview on worker exposure to diesel particulate matter (DPM) and to discuss the effect of control technology on that exposure. Worker exposure has been assessed from in-mine diesel particulate measurements. The effect of control technology has been evaluated by a systems approach, which includes engine emission rate, mine ventilation system, and the effectiveness of engine after treatment devices. Studies conducted by the Mine Safety and Health Administration and the Bureau of Mines show that the primary means currently employed by the mining industry to control worker exposure to DPM include mine design, ventilation, engine maintenance, and the use of low sulfur fuel. Additional reductions in exposure can be obtained through the use of electronic engine technology. Commercially available after treatment devices are capable of reducing DPM by 25 to 95 percent. Reductions in exposure to DPM are dependent on the application of available engine emission control technology and modifications to mine ventilation systems. © 1997, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. entry.dc:title: Impact of coal surface mining on three Ohio watersheds - Surface-water hydrology
entry.dc:creator: Bonta J.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of the American Water Resources Association
entry.dc:description: A study was conducted to determine the effects of mining and reclaiming originally undisturbed watersheds on surface-water hydrology in three small experimental watersheds in Ohio. Approximately six years of data were collected at each site, with differing lengths of premining (Phase 1), mining and reclamation (Phase 2), and post-reclamation (Phase 3) periods. Mining and reclamation activities showed no consistent pattern in base-flow, and caused slightly more frequent higher daily flow volumes. Phase 2 activities can cause reductions in seasonal variation in double mass curves compared with Phase 1. Restoration of seasonal variations was noticeably apparent at one site during Phase 3. The responses of the watersheds to rainfall intensities causing larger peak flow rates generally decreased due to mining and reclamation, but tended to exceed responses observed in Phase I during Phase 3. Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) curve numbers increased due to mining and reclamation (Phase 2), ranging from 83 to 91. During Phase 3, curve numbers remained approximately constant from Phase 2, ranging from 87 to 91.

entry.dc:title: An introduction to the integrated design of surface mine haul roads
entry.dc:creator: Thompson R.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
entry.dc:description: The world-wide expansion of surface mining has led to the development of very large off-highway trucks currently capable of hauling payloads in excess of 160t. Typical axle loads ranging from 110t to 170t are applied to haul roads that have been, at best, empirically designed on the premise of "satisfactory" or "failed", both in terms of structure and function of the road. The use of these empirical pavement design techniques will prove inadequate when high axle loads are encountered. Not only will the maintenance costs of existing haul roads of inadequate thickness increase, but vehicle operating and maintenance costs will also increase prohibitively. Under these conditions there is thus a clearly defined need for improved construction and management techniques for flexible mine haul roads, appropriate for the wheel loads of vehicles now in use. The aim of this paper is to introduce developments in haul road structural, functional and maintenance design and management which overcome the limitations associated with the previously empirical design techniques and to show how these developments are combined into an integrated design strategy combining construction techniques, available material and road maintenance equipment with hauler choice to realise a reduction in haulage and road maintenance costs. Future contributions will enumerate on the fundamental haul road structural, functional and maintenance design and management research from which these developments originated.

entry.dc:title: Surface mining equipment cost analysis with a developed linear break even model
entry.dc:creator: Cebesoy T.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
entry.dc:description: As the international surface mining industry proceeds into twenty first century, surface operation throughout the world will increasingly encounter many problems in terms of economic viability and in such situations, true cost analysis techniques taking into account time value of money approach have gained more important than ever before. Linear break even model as a true cost analysis model contributes an important role in surface mining equipment cost analysis. As an illustration, this paper introduces a linear break even model developed for equipment replacement analysis and in so doing, also the adaptation of two linear models which will be used in estimating equipment operating cost over time are examined in detail. Hence the paper is concluded with a given numerical example.

entry.dc:title: Achieving effective telerobotic control of industrial equipment
entry.dc:creator: Hunter D.
entry.dc:description: Equipment which may be remotely operated, has some degree of on-board intelligence, and which for periods of time may operate autonomously, is referred to as telerobotic. Recent advances in electronics, computers and hydraulic equipment have dramatically reduced the cost and simplified the process of converting standard industrial equipment to telerobotic control. The benefits of telerobotic equipment include improved safety by removing the operator from dangerous situations, reduced maintenance costs and increased productivity. This technology has been proven in various military, nuclear, and police applications. The surface mining industry has expressed an interest in automation and is characterized by a willingness to use remotely operated equipment, however, the majority of telerobotic equipment currently in use is experimental or prototypical. Potential applications of telerobotic equipment for surface mining include remote operation of equipment near dangerous highwalls and other unsafe areas, utilization of robotic trucks for routine hauling operations, and control of jointed equipment In addition, component technologies of telerobotic systems are relevant to various forms of condition monitoring, operator feedback systems, and vehicle positioning. Attention must now be directed toward resolving more complex problems associated with enhancing feedback to the operator, improving the man/machine interface, and ultimately, improving efficiency. Removal of the human operator from the work site introduces significant complications in replacing the sensory inputs that an operator normally uses to efficiently run his machinery. These can be difficult to define and even more difficult to replicate remotely and may include restrictions pertaining to vision, hearing, and touch. In cooperation with Defence Research Establishment Suffield and the Alberta Research Council, Robotech Industries Ltd. is pursuing the development of additional technologies to further enhance an operator's ability to control remote telerobotic equipment. These developments include a head-mounted display, additional control station displays and improvements to coordinated motion control software. Prototypes of these developments are expected to be completed and tested by the fourth quarter of 1997.
entry.authkeywords: Automation | Surface mining | Telerobotic control | Telerobotic equipment

entry.dc:title: Materials for controlling wear in surface mining
entry.dc:creator: Llewellyn R.
entry.dc:description: It has been estimated conservatively that the costs of wear damage and friction in the Canadian mining and mineral processing industry amount to over one billion dollars per year. These are mainly incurred through the repair or replacement of worn parts and production losses from related equipment downtime. The selection and application of the most appropriate wear protection components and systems, can thus have a very significant influence on productivity, profitability and global competitiveness. Details are presented of the wide diversity of materials used to counteract the varied and often complex wear attack mechanisms that occur in surface mining. The majority are various forms of steels and irons with generally very high hardness. However, they also include relatively soft elastomers and polymeric products. The main characteristics and applications of the different classes are reviewed. Case studies record significant performance improvements achieved through more judicious selections. Finally, some new developments which reduce maintenance charges by substantially increasing wear component life, are described.
entry.authkeywords: Abrasion | Elastomers | Erosion | Friction | Surface mining | Wear

entry.dc:title: Mining process optimization and quality control by computer-aided development planning in surface mining
entry.dc:creator: Emons A.
entry.dc:description: This paper briefly describes how to use specialized mining software in order to optimize the mining process and quality output. Before simulating future mining operations, two models have to be set up. One model which describes the actual mining situation by using survey data, whilst the second model represents the deposit, using borehole data and other available geological information such as existing cross-sections. By using geostatistical modules, a block model can be built up which acts as a spatial data base and allows all necessary data for the mine scheduling processes to be calculated and visualized.

entry.dc:title: An overview of surface mining in India
entry.dc:creator: Singh V.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: In the last two decades, surface mining has witnessed significant expansion. Currently, it contributes for more than 70% of the mineral production volume. A number of large and deep open pit mines have come up which are highly capital-intensive. All efforts should be made to increase the productivity by economies of scale, equipment utilisation, optimum slope design and by the adoption of suitable reclamation techniques to avoid environmental degradation. The paper discusses the present scenario in open pit mining and also suggests the ways and means to improve the productivity in the present liberalization period.

entry.dc:title: Appearance of wear in brown coal surface mining - reduction of wear by application of modern materials technology
entry.dc:creator: van den Heuvel B.
entry.dc:description: A number of modern materials technology researches have been carried out to improve wear behavior in excavators. The existence of different wear types and wear parameters complicates the wear problem and presents great difficulties in material selection. St 37, a structural steel with a high hardness number, was proven effective for buckets and their wearing parts, while deposition welding with plasma powder demonstrated longer service life and reduced costs for bucket replacement. However, the application of these developments are limited and unsuccessful for other wear parameters.

entry.dc:title: Supervisory control systems and the intelligent mine - A new tool for productivity improvement in surface mining
entry.dc:creator: Olivieri F.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
entry.dc:description: In the late 70's Modular implemented its first mine management system, called DISPATCH, for haulage optimization in open pit mines. Since that time, this system has been placed in over 75 mines worldwide. Initially just used for dispatching haul trucks, the system has evolved to provide complete, real-time and historical production data and maintenance data. It also allows connection to onboard PLCs (programmable logic controllers) supplied by major equipment manufacturers for monitoring machine data and global positioning systems (GPS). The DISPATCH mine management system has developed into the cornerstone of these operations. Every ton dug and every second worked is counted. Each equipment work assignment is optimized. Global positioning systems and on-board monitoring computers are laying the groundwork for video arcade age mines. The advances in equipment electronics technology over the pasl five years has been tremendous. Who knows how our mines will look after the next five years. How about a glimpse into the future? First a little background history.

entry.dc:title: Surface mining collaborative research initiatives: a progress report
entry.dc:creator: Muirhead I.
entry.dc:description: Over the past year or so, a number of mining companies have been meeting to examine the role of research in surface mining and, in particular, how to establish a collaborative research effort for the surface mining industry. A review has been completed which has identified the topics that are of interest to the surface mining companies for undertaking collaborative research. This has identified key subject areas such as Operations & Equipment; Maintenance; Environment & Reclamation; and Stability. Specific research projects for the initial research effort have been selected which include Wireless Data Communications, Analysis and Management; Application of GPS in Mining; and Tires for Heavy Haulers. In addition, attention has also been focussed on finding a suitable low cost, but effective, organization to coordinate and manage the collaborative research. The recently formed CONRAD Organization (Canadian Oilsands Network for Research and Development) appears to be a suitable candidate and discussions are ongoing with that group. This paper provides a summary of the review of surface mining research needs and of the status of the establishment of a collaborative research body for surface mining.

entry.dc:title: Results of in-situ measurement of breaking characteristics of rocks in lignite surface mines
entry.dc:creator: Jurman J.
entry.prism:publicationName: Prace Naukowe Instytutu Gornictwa Politechniki Wroclawskiej
entry.dc:description: The breaking characteristics of rock is expressed for individual excavation technologies, and, with regard to differences of individual processes, there is no universal criterion of such breaking evaluation. A demand for information quality and quantity increase in a sense of the breaking characteristics with surface mining, led to the consideration of using drilling process monitoring results that could be applied easily on given terms. However, it means the expression of a correlation between when drilling = drillability, and between breaking when drilling with a rotary excavator = digging resistance. On the basis of operational measurements, the problem analysis was performed and possibilities of the solution were outlined.

entry.dc:title: Development of surface mining technology and operation management in the Rhineland lignite basin
entry.dc:creator: Oster A.
entry.prism:publicationName: Prace Naukowe Instytutu Gornictwa Politechniki Wroclawskiej
entry.dc:description: The largest German lignite deposit is found to the west of the city of Cologne, Rhineland. The lignite is mined in four opencast mines with a total capacity of 110 - 120 Mt/a. The gradual deterioration of mining conditions has been encountered by concentrating lignite recovery in very four mines, implementing new concepts in the mine design and operation and realizing numerous technical and organizational innovations. All this contributed to a notable increase in productivity of the mines, which allows competition on the energy market. Since the seventies, bucket wheel excavators, stackers and belt conveyors with a capacity of 240.000 m<sup>3</sup>+t/d have been in use which since then have proven their versatility even in difficult conditions. For the effective operation of this equipment, each mine is run via a modern electronic monitoring and communication center.

entry.dc:creator: Piatkowiak N.
entry.prism:publicationName: Prace Naukowe Instytutu Gornictwa Politechniki Wroclawskiej
entry.dc:description: Surface mining of brown coal deposits leaves dumping grounds that need to be returned to the natural environment. They often contain materials that are harmful or potentially harmful to the environment. The location of such materials is usually not known. An attempt has been made to define and classify those harmful and potentially harmful wastes. The need for a unified classification and assessment model has. Such a model should be applied, in a legislative form, all over Germany. Geotechnical parameters should be included as a significant part of the model.

entry.dc:title: Pushing the envelope
entry.dc:creator: Whiteway P.
entry.dc:description: Since 1978, Syncrude Canada has acquired a wealth of operating experience in Alberta's tough oil sands environment. Today, the company's owners are excited about investing in expansion, and Syncrude is utilizing technology that should enable the company to mine sands further removed than ever before from its processing complex. The success of the project will allow even more of the huge Athabasca oil sand deposit to be mined using surface mining methods and owners will realize their target of a 12% return on capital invested.
